utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-05-87-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, can I take the appearance for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm Tom Hannis, appearing on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm joined today by our case manager Tamara Margitic on my right; on my left, trial attorney Christina Moeller; and behind me, trial attorney Mathias Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. This is a Status Conference in the conjoined case of Milutinovic and others and it involves, at the moment, six accused, all of whom are on provisional release. So as I take the appearances for the Defence, I would like to confirm your appearance and also assure me that your client is aware of the Status Conference taking place and has authorised you to conduct it on his behalf in his absence. So can I take the appearances in turn, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Eugene O'Sullivan and Slobodan Zecevic, appearing for Mr. Milutinovic, who is not present this morning, who is aware of this Status Conference and waives his right to be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Toma Fila and I appear with Mr. Vladimir Petrovic, representing the Defence counsel of Mr. Sainovic, who is aware that we're holding a Status Conference today and has authorised to us conduct the proceedings on his behalf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Tomislav Visnjic, an attorney, and I represent General Ojdanic, who is aware of the Status Conference being held today and has waived his right to attend in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm John Ackerman and I'm here with Aleksandar Aleksic, my co-counsel, and General Pavkovic is aware of this conference and has authorised us to proceed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac. I represent General Vladimir Lazarevic. Together with me is my colleague Mr. Milan Petrovic. General Lazarevic is aware of this Status Conference being held today, and he is waiving his right to attend in person and has authorised me to represent him at today's Status Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Dragan Ivetic on behalf of the Defence of General Sreten Lukic. General Lukic is apprised of today's proceedings. He, with full knowledge, has waived his appearance and has authorised myself to appear on his behalf for today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. And I should record also that Mr. Scudder contacted me personally to indicate the difficulty about his attendance today, and I authorised the Status Conference to proceed in his absence also. Now, yesterday afternoon we had a 65 ter Conference. I suppose it's fairly easy in the atmosphere of fruitful discussion to say just how cooperative things appeared to be at that time among everyone, but having reflected on the matter overnight, I think it right to record now publicly what seemed to me to be an extremely successful discussion and to acknowledge the cooperation of all parties on both sides in efforts to get this case underway as a trial at the earliest reasonable opportunity. In saying that, I don't mean for a minute to pre-judge what I know will be submissions that counsel will wish to make about the projected dates. I simply at this stage acknowledge I think everyone's goodwill towards achieving as early a trial date as is reasonable and fair. A number of matters were discussed yesterday, and the position in most of them was fairly clear. I think it right, though, to deal with a number of them in the context of the Status Conference just to give each of us an opportunity to review what appeared to be decided yesterday. The first thing I think I want to do is acknowledge what's outstanding. A recent decision of the Trial Chamber dealt with challenges to the proposed amended indictment or objections to the proposed amended indictment, and at the moment the ball is in the court of the Prosecution on that one to produce a further revised indictment. Mr. Hannis indicated yesterday that that would be forthcoming within the next few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I believe our date is Wednesday, the 5th of April, and we anticipate filing on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It was also noted that the additional features in this indictment would be clearly identified with translation in mind, and I indicated that I would discuss the question of translation with CLSS with a view to ensuring that all counsel have a copy of the indictment in its entirety in B/C/S as quickly as possible, and I shall undertake that at the beginning of the week, once I see what is actually involved. The second thing that is outstanding is an appeal by the United States, I think, in relation to one interlocutory matter, and I will simply report to the Appeals Chamber the importance of having the matter dealt with as quickly as possible. My understanding is that there is nothing required of the parties, that everything is in hand, and it's simply a question of producing a decision. The third outstanding matter was one raised by Mr. Ackerman, who indicated to me that there had been discussions among counsel with a view to formulating specific and all-inclusive requests for material, documentary material, on behalf of the Defence and that within the next ten days appropriate requests would be made. And I indicated to him then that he should bear in mind the impending nature of the trial when deciding whether it might be necessary to invoke the Court's assistance in terms of Rule 54 bis in relation to any requests made. So that is a matter of which the Court has notice. And the fourth outstanding matter, I think the final one, related to certain protective measures already requested and then withdrawn, and that matter was left on the basis that Mr. Hannis would revive it by making a fresh filing in the light of the up-to-date information he indicated he had. He also indicated that there may be protective measures sought for other witnesses not yet intimated in full to the Defence, and I urged him, and he agreed, to treat that as a matter of urgency. Now, unless counsel can recollect any outstanding issue that requires a determination, then I think that covers the matters we discussed which yet require resolution. All right. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: There was one other matter that you asked us on the Defence side to consider. That was a date for the next 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I come back to that, if you don't mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got that particularly in mind. I was thinking more of things that require action over which I don't at the moment have any control. That takes me to the question of Prosecution witnesses. There were a few loose ends, I think, left yesterday, Mr. Hannis, so I think everyone would be grateful for as specific an indication as you can give now of the number of witnesses you anticipate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, our most recent calculation had us anticipating calling some 80, 8-0, witnesses as live witnesses. We had another 90 witnesses we proposed to submit under Rule 92 bis. And in addition, we have now, I believe, 11 experts we're proposing. As we indicated to you yesterday, we do no longer intend to call Mr. Torkildsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may actually be ten. Does that not reduce it to ten?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour. I did my math wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The expert question I'll come back to, but I think I can note now that you have apparently disclosed all the anticipated material in relation to each of the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I did indicate yesterday that with Mr. Coo we might file a supplement based on some of the new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He was the only one. Now, going back to your other witnesses, how many of these witnesses have not yet been disclosed to the Defence? Can you tell me roughly even the number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, of -- I haven't calculated that because as some of what we were doing was replacing some witnesses. I know that previously we had said I think we were going to have 66 live witnesses and about the same number of viva voce -- of 92 bis. That number increased so the number may be something in the neighbourhood of 20 live and 20 or 30 92 bis, but that's a very tentative number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's quite a large number of witnesses, and it seems to me that there can be no justification for not disclosing immediately all the material, all the supporting material relating to these witnesses unless there are issues of protection involved. Now, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do accept that, Your Honour. I would indicate that for these additional numbers I'm confident that a number of them, their statements have already been disclosed, they just weren't previously identified as a witness we intended to call at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I can immediately understand the concern of Defence counsel about the vagueness of this, so I really need to have an undertaking from you, Mr. Hannis, that within a week of today they'll have everything in relation to which you do not envisage seeking protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will undertake to do that, Your Honour, and if I have a time problem, I will seek relief from you, if there's any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. I think you also owe it to everyone now to make it clear within the same time scale the number of witnesses and the general nature of their evidence for whom protective measures are to be sought and to take steps to have that resolved now so that appropriate disclosure can be made at the earliest possible date. Now, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, would you -- would you try to please apply the same time scale to at least indicating what the position is and formulating an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we also discussed the potential length of the trial, and I think that there are loose ends in respect of that that can't be tied up today. I hope that I accurately reflect what happened yesterday when I say that you are unlikely to have 80 witnesses whose evidence in chief is given viva voce in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We anticipate trying to make good use of Rule 89(F).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. And we had, I hope, a -- I indicated to you my understanding of where difficulties can arise when a witness's evidence appears to be unbalanced in the sense that the bulk of his oral evidence is given in cross-examination, but I indicated that the Court would be alert to that, and we'd expect that where issues had been raised in cross-examination, the Prosecution would deal with any foreseen difficulties about the way in which a witness was apparently presented by dealing with the matter in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point on that, Your Honour, and that's a matter that we intend to deal with. Part of it will depend on the personalities involved in the actual trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you also gave me an estimate of the time that you envisaged using to present the Prosecution case. Can you remind me of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe we said that was 18 weeks, Your Honour. That's simply for the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is that on the basis of the 80 viva voce witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So that matter is obviously subject to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I invited you to have particular regard to the fact that the Prosecution, in presenting the Kosovo phase of the Milosevic indictment, took only 122 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I recall that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As against 18 weeks I think is 360 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, based on a calculation of 20-hour weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I think it's an important factor to bear in mind that the whole of the Prosecution case over the three indictments in Milosevic took 360 hours, roughly the equivalent of what you envisage for the presentation of the Prosecution case in this case. I appreciate we have six accused, but I think I reminded you yesterday that the crime scenes are the same for all of them and the only separate individual issue will be criminal responsibility, and it's not clear to me that that's by any means the bulk of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. So I make it clear to you now that I have a different view of the likely time scale of the Prosecution case, even allowing for cross-examination. Mr. Fila made it clear that it's the plan of all counsel here to agree in advance of the presentation of each witness which counsel will take principal responsibility for cross-examining the witness with a view to the expeditious presentation of that evidence. And having that in mind, it does seem to me that 360 hours may be a closer estimate of the time necessary for the whole Prosecution case, including cross-examination and re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree, and I was pleased to hear that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So we're now looking, I think, at a rather different picture from the one that has been in mind for this case. The 28 months that were envisaged I expect to be substantially reduced. Nothing more, I think, need be said about Prosecution expert witnesses, but I would like, I think, Mr. O'Sullivan to remind me of the position taken by the Defence in relation to their preparation of expert witnesses. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yesterday the counsel for the Defence met, and we now know that there are ten experts proposed by the Prosecution, and for six of those experts we agree that we can call one expert in reply. For six of the ten. The other four, we're still -- we still have to work among us to see whether we will have one or more experts in the other four areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I suggested to you that you might reflect upon the time at which you would anticipate reports being available and whether disclosure of the Defence expert position before the Prosecution expert gave evidence might be conducive to cutting down the areas in dispute. Now, have you given any more consideration to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We haven't discussed that jointly, and quite frankly, I'm opposed to that, speaking for myself at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How do you envisage dealing with an expert? By that I mean instructing him finally before he gives you his final report? You envisage doing that after the Prosecution expert has given evidence or at some earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At an earlier stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But holding on to the material until you've heard the Prosecution's expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that -- that fits into a -- it depends. I can only speak for myself and my client in relation to this at this point. That is our -- that will fit into our trial and Defence strategy, yes, that determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Under the Rules, of course, our expert can follow the proceedings when the Prosecution's expert is testifying. That much is an exception to the Rule too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, jurisdictions all over the world have different approaches, as I understand it, to the extent to which one expert can follow the evidence of another. I see no difficulty with the idea that a Defence expert should follow the evidence of a Prosecution expert, but I have a bit more difficulty with the idea that in every case it should be, well, let's wait and see before we try to cut down the areas in dispute, and I think I do have certain power in relation to experts which I don't have in relation to the disclosure of other Defence witnesses which I may decide to exercise, and I'm interested to have your comments before I make any decision on this. And what I'm -- the message I'm getting is, no, we'll be fully prepared by the time the Prosecution expert gives evidence. We'll have our report, but we think it's right to hold on to it until afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not criticising, I'm just trying to get the picture. And I understand you clearly on that, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can't say that the report -- a Defence expert report will necessarily be completed by the time the Prosecution expert testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can't say that. That's the only proviso I would add to what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I acknowledge certainly the cooperation among counsel to try to cut down the number of experts. That's encouraging. But there may even be cases, I suggest to you, as you prepare in which there may be scope for mutual disclosure with the Prosecution with a view to identifying how little is actually in dispute between you. And indeed, even if it doesn't involve disclosure, it might be a good idea, once you have more or less finalised your own expert's position, to tell the Prosecution what's not in dispute so that -- and hold back, if you think tactically that's the right thing to do, as little as possible in everyone's interest. I just encourage you to think about these things as we make progress. Now, does any other Defence counsel wish to comment on expert witnesses at all? Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to give a clarification regarding the comment you made just now about the mutual agreement among counsel, that only one Defence counsel will be cross-examining on behalf of all. I wish to say on behalf of our client that we did not reach such an agreement. Of course we will discuss it among us, but at this point no such agreement has been reached among us, and we will probably act on a witness-by-witness basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's the way I put it, then it was a misrepresentation of what Mr. Ackerman actually said. What I hope I said was that he indicated that you would get together and decide which counsel should be the lead cross-examiner in relation to each witness, reserving the right - and I should have made that absolutely clear - reserving the right to all other Defence counsel to raise issues that they felt had to be individually explored on behalf of their clients. So I fully understand that and I'm sorry about the misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was one other thing I wanted you to make clear about Defence experts, and I think it was you that raised it yesterday, and that was the question of funding and whether there are advantages to be gained in relation to funding by combining your resources. Now, can you clarify that for me again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will make a submission to the Registry requesting some sort of merging of funds available to Defence regarding experts. But the comment you just made leads me to think of my reasoning, previous reasoning, about the financing of experts. The Tribunal limits the financing of expert evidence in pre-trial stage and the trial stage, according to the information we got from the Registry. For instance, experts are financed with one lump sum in the pre-trial stage, another lump sum during the trial stage, depending on the size and contents of the report. We will probably need to consult again with the Registry whether the system indeed allows for this. This adds only one technical difficulty to the idea you voiced just now. Otherwise, I completely agree with it, and I don't think there will be any obstacles to doing it in this trial in the way you suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I just -- I just want to record my appreciation of the efforts that are being made to cut down the number of experts used in this case, and I hope the Registry are alert to the importance of assisting counsel so far as they can in that exercise. I appreciate the difficulty for all concerned but I would encourage them to recognise particularly the efforts that have been made in this case. Now, that concludes my review of the position in relation to witnesses, subject to anything any counsel wishes to say on the matter before I move to a completely separate issue. All right. I take it that silence indicates there's nothing else to be reviewed on that score. I want now to turn to, as I say, a completely separate issue which I alerted three of the counsel here to be in a position to address today, and I did so for a particular reason. The Registry has drawn to the attention of the Trial Chamber what might be seen as activity on the part of three of the accused which may not be consistent with the terms on which they were provisionally released. Now, I'm raising it with you as a general point. I'm purely concerned about any misunderstanding that there may be in general about the terms on which there is provisional release and how these terms are dealt with should there be a need to review them because of unexpected events or developments. I'm not regarding this at this stage as a complaint that I have to address, but I was anxious to have as much information as you feel able to give me about the circumstances so that I can reassure myself that there isn't a general problem which requires to be addressed in relation to the future position of the accused or indeed any other accused on provisional release in Serbia. Now, the three accused referred to were Sainovic, Ojdanic, and Pavkovic. So, Mr. Fila, can I ask you if you can be of assistance to me in clarifying this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are here in this courtroom in order to tell each other the truth and to respect one another. I'm saying this at the outset meaning that if any error has been made, I am responsible for one part of that error and the government of Serbia for another. I am unable to provide any additional documents because we were only notified on Tuesday and we were flying on Wednesday, and at the request of the Interior Ministry -- when I made the request to the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence, they said the documents were confidential and they would provide them to you if necessary. Namely, those are police reports confirming that all the three accused had police escort when they travelled and that the distance in question is 30 kilometres, not 60, as you were notified. It's the territory of the city of Belgrade, which is 20 kilometres away from the site in Pozarevac, 20 kilometres. I do wish to assist you in clarifying this matter. As you can see, the letter addressed to the Ministry of Justice was signed by me because I am the one who is responsible for the possible violation of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know there is a letter but I have deliberately not read it yet because there was too much happening before I came in here this morning. Let me have a moment to read the letter that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have their letter. You have only the letter that I wrote, and you are -- you also have the reply from the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Fila, I have a copy of the letter to the Ministry of Justice. That's the document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. And you should also have the reply from the Ministry of Justice granting me approval, and I will now explain, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I haven't been given that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reply is in the bundle given you by the Registry. Page 1710. That's the material sent to you by the Registry. I have a copy if you need one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clear up confusion, if you look at the original document provided by the Registry, the letter is attached to it. It's not something that was supplied today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you just look at the Registry's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fila, the page number again, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1710. That's a reply. Before I embarked on writing that letter, I asked verbally if there had been such precedence before, and I was told that the interpretation of your decisions is such that when emergencies are in question - baptism, funeral, wedding, or something similar which requires an absence of several hours or maybe a night - it is the discretionary right of the Ministry of Justice, together with the Ministry of the Interior, to grant approval. Let me correct myself: It is allowed for the accused to be absent for a day, but not a night. And in that case they are given police escort, which has been observed in this case. After receiving this clarification, I wrote to the minister of justice, and now I am being asked why I hadn't asked for your approval as well. That's my mistake. The death of Mr. Milosevic was sudden. It created enormous outcry in the media. And I believe that under the circumstances this travel of 20 kilometres cannot be considered as a grave violation of the terms of provisional release, and I think you have better, more urgent business to attend to than dealing with this travel, this journey of only 20 kilometres of half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I hope I made it clear to you at the outset that I'm not looking at it from that point of view. I'm looking at it from the general issue point of view. In other words, is there a problem here in general about how these conditions are being interpreted? This -- I express no view on what happened in this instance, but I can envisage that if this sort of thing is not addressed and the position clarified, that something unfortunate could happen, and I want to avoid that eventuality.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is there anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to tell you what it looks like. The Ministry of Justice believes that it is possible to grant approval for several hours, but certainly not more than 12. The minister of police is then notified, and he designates police escort. Generally speaking, they are under police supervision, under surveillance, round the clock. They cannot leave their apartments without police escort, even when they are going to see their counsel. When Mr. Sainovic is going to meetings with me, he goes under police escort. That not only provides surveillance but also prevents attacks, et cetera. So the way we understand it, it is not necessary to summon the Trial Chamber to decide on matters like this for such a small, short absence. You will see from the report that you will receive and that I haven't received because they explained it's confidential and it's not our business to know how the police organises their work. That is all I can tell you. And if there are any omissions on our part, I am entirely responsible, not Mr. Sainovic. Death is a -- an important occasion in our Orthodox Christian church. And if Slobodan Milosevic hadn't been in question, this would never have occurred. Can I be of assistance in any other way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you're right, that it shouldn't be necessary to summon the Trial Chamber to decide on matters like this, then it's important that that is well known and that the ground rules for such situations are clear. On the other hand, if they weren't clear, then it could be said that the strict terms of the -- of the conditions apply, and it's that sort of uncertainty that I'm anxious to avoid. As it turns out, for all I -- from all I have heard, the funeral passed off reasonably well, but you could imagine other circumstances in the -- anywhere in the Balkan region where something unfortunate happened. Gosh, it happens at football matches every night. So there are foreseeable potential consequences for even minor excursions like this, and therefore I think it is important that the position is clear and that the matter's not left in doubt. However, I'm grateful to you for explaining the position to me. Mr. Visnjic, is there anything you need to add to this or do you feel the need to explain the position of Mr. Ojdanic in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly. On behalf of General Ojdanic, I submitted my request on the 16th of March around 1400 hours to the Ministry of Justice, and around 1600 hours I received their reply on the same date, granting approval for him to attend the funeral that was held on the 17th of March. I submitted that document. I filed it. What I wish to say is that I actually support this position of the Ministry of Justice, although it's the first time that my client has availed myself of that particular possibility in almost one year that he has been on provisional release. On one previous occasion, my client absented himself from Belgrade for treatment, and on that occasion we had approval from the Trial Chamber. However, under these circumstances, I believe the position of the Ministry of Justice is completely reasonable, because otherwise I think this Trial Chamber would be completely snowed under similar requests, very minor, and would cause unnecessary outlay of resources that can be much better spent, and we would be facing an absurd situation over details like the one I recently found about. One of the accused on provisional release, for instance, had to visit a doctor that is only one kilometre away from what is formally considered the territory of the city of Belgrade, and that required him to request special permission. That is an indication that maybe the procedure should be simplified. But even in this case, the matter was completely under the control of the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior, which as my colleague pointed out, carries out round-the-clock surveillance. In order to provide you with a complete picture, my client was specifically told by his escort that if his escort does not get permission from the Ministry of the Interior, that is the Ministry of Police, he would be arrested if he leaves the territory specifically designated by the terms of provisional release. So we have two ministries exercising control, and both these ministries have accordingly notified the Ministry of Finance. So we cannot say that this travel of our clients violated the guarantees provided by the State or that it was self-willed or that it jeopardised the safety of any victims or witnesses or that it indeed violated any of the restrictions imposed by the terms of provisional release. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Visnjic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Visnjic, what it boils down to is an interpretation of the first condition that applies to each of these provisional release orders. A ministry statement, according to the Registrar, was to the effect that the obligation was not to leave the territory of the city of Belgrade without the approval of the ministry. There's nothing in these orders that authorises the ministry to give such approval. Now, I understand all you're saying about how you might view this as a -- as a technicality or as a sensible course of action or whatever, but in the end of the day, the ministry may have abrogated to themselves authority which, if they really wanted to have it, they should have been asking the Tribunal to grant them, rather than simply causing confusion by acting in what on the face of it is in breach of the terms in which each of the accused was released. So I acknowledge that nothing in particular appears to have occurred that had any adverse effect, but, nevertheless, as I emphasised to Mr. Fila, it's important that these things are not left in doubt and uncertainty. Anyway, thank you for your comments. Mr. Ackerman, is there anything you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think you understand the situation very clearly. Only -- I'll only say this: I have provided with -- to you today the letter requesting permission for my client to -- to travel and the letter from the ministry authorising it, so that, at least in his mind, he was in compliance with -- with the requirements. He's recently released and walked into a situation where this had apparently become a rather standard practice. Whether or not that needs to be addressed or not is a matter, I suppose, that needs to be taken up by the Judges. It seems to me that the Tribunal relies upon the government of, in this case Serbia, and the police and the Justice Ministry to a great extent in enforcing the terms of provisional release, and it would seem that a bit of discretion might be appropriate in that regard because of matters that come up rather quickly and can be dealt with. It's my observation that they go beyond what is required by the Judges. The -- each of the persons on provisional release is under 24-hour police surveillance. There are police with them constantly. They can't go anywhere without police being with them, and so it's not just that they check in to the police once a day; they're with them all the time. So I think it's not a problem, but if the Tribunal wants to instruct the Ministry of Justice that they are not authorised to issue these permissions, I think that's what should happen, but I don't think it's anything to do with our clients.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I can tell you I have experience of applications being made to the Trial Chamber for variation of conditions for funerals, so it's plain that others have taken a different view of what the conditions require. Anyway, I'm very grateful to all three counsel for explaining the position. Mr. Hannis, I wasn't anticipating that you would necessarily have anything to say on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I realise it's primarily a matter between the Court and the accused, but I did have a comment, if you're willing me -- if you're willing to permit me to make one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm certainly not going to prevent you, but as long as it's relevant to the general point I'm considering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope it will be. I hope that you will find that it is. My concern, Your Honour, is that there appears to be a fundamental disconnect or misunderstanding here. I agree that looking at the incident itself, for example, with Mr. Fila's client travelling that sort distance for that short time under the circumstances, certainly if the application had been made to the Court, I anticipate there would be no problem and it would have been granted. My problem is, as you pointed, the release conditions are that they are not to leave the territory. There is no exception, there is no delegation of this Court's authority to the Ministry of Justice in Serbia, and that's my concern. They've taken it upon themselves, apparently, without any consultation with the Court, to do that. In addition, I do note I was handed some documents this morning from co-counsel for Mr. Pavkovic indicating that apparently has been made requests for and been granted permission to travel on five other occasions prior to the funeral outside the city, and at least on one of those occasions it appears the permission was not just until midnight but for a period of 24 hours, and date of travel was indicated as "when needed." That's a little broader discretion. Those particular requests I think were not signed by Minister Stojkovic but, rather, a person who is described as State Secretary Bjelica. And these were matters that were not in the Registrar's report but I think they should come to your attention as well on the issue of the general point. I would request, Your Honour, that you consider the possibility of having the minister of justice appear before you to make sure that there's a clear understanding of where the authority lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. It would be helpful if you gave copies of these documents to the court registrar. On the -- we already have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They already have them. We gave them to everyone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The purpose was to show that this was a pattern that had developed and not some aberration that the funeral --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't intend personally to invite the ministry to appear here or indeed make representations. I simply wish to identify whether there is a general issue. I think there is one. I intend now to report the information I've gleaned to the Trial Chamber, but I suspect that what they'll want to do is simply report it back to the Registry, and the Registry can then decide what, if any, course is appropriate in relation to this. Whether it's simply to alert Trial Chambers to deal with it individually or whether it's a policy matter that needs to be dealt with in general will be for others within the Tribunal to decide. Mine was a fact-finding mission this morning, and I think that you also, Mr. Hannis, have supplemented my knowledge, and I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One last point, Your Honour. Part of my concern and request regarding perhaps having the minister here to make it clear is that one of the media stories about this account quoted the Deputy Prime Minister as saying that no one in the government given permission. So internally that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am aware of that from the submission but I don't consider it's for me in my context of my role as the Pre-Trial Judge in this case to take the matter up with the ministry directly. I certainly won't be doing that. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, had Mr. Hannis not raised the subject, although I did expect the subject to be broached, the Vice-Prime Minister's -- Deputy Prime Minister's statement, so I asked what this was about. The Vice-Premier said that the government did not make a decision on the matter. And the government of Serbia did not indeed make a decision. I checked that out, so please believe me that I'm telling you the truth when I say this, because the government does not resolve questions of this kind. These are questions that are resolved by the minister of justice together with the minister of the interior. So that Mr. Labu [phoen] said something which has nothing to do with him, and he does have occasion to speak about things he doesn't know about. The Hague Tribunal, for example. It doesn't come under his remit. And in 1993 he said, for example, that these three accused, Pavkovic, Lukic, and - what was the third's name? - Lazarevic, were accused because Sainovic and Ojdanic had given their names to the Prosecutor. That same Vice-Premier said that. But we have a government that we -- the kind of government we have and most frequently people are talking about things they know nothing about, but that's the situation, so thank you, I needed to make that additional explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. I hope when we get to the trial that we'll be able to concentrate on forensic rather than political issues. I'll turn now to the question of timetabling for the future conduct of the pre-trial phase and also the trial itself, and I think I should hear first of all from Mr. O'Sullivan who reminded me earlier of my request that we should try to identify a date for the next 65 ter conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, yesterday you asked us to consider when may be an appropriate date to hold the next 65 ter. We did discuss that, and we can inform you that a convenient date for us is Wednesday, the 19th of April. We think that that -- having it sooner rather than later is important, and the 19th of April doesn't conflict with either the Western or Eastern Easters. It falls between the two. So from our side it's a date in all regards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm feeling particularly guilty now. You'll realise how limited are the holidays for Judges in this Tribunal, and apart from the recesses, we have two weeks which we can identify for ourselves, and this Trial Chamber identified that week, because it coincided with Easter Monday, as the week off. It would be very helpful to me if it wasn't the 19th of April. If we were to go into the following week --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe we can inform you little bit -- I mean after Status Conference, when we discuss about possible dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any date the following week would be fine, if that can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's better we inform you after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as I explained to you yesterday, I tried to formulate a provisional timetable based on the date at which I thought it was reasonable to try to begin this trial, and I want to explain exactly what -- again what my thinking on this was. The Court recess is slightly movable for Trial Chambers, so it can fit within a period of five weeks but it's a three-week period in itself, and the core three-week period which this Trial Chamber has to recognise on this occasion is from the 15th of July until the 6th of August. It seemed to me that if this trial was to be -- because of its size, number of accused, number of personnel, just general logistical issues, if we were to be sure of having the trial up and running properly immediately after the recess, then we had to have all formalities out of the way before the recess and we had to have the trial actually under way before the recess. So I identified the date for the commencement of the trial as the 10th of July. I had in mind that if there was to be an opening from the Prosecution, that's when it would be. I had in mind that hopefully evidence presented then would not be so controversial as to cause difficulty for any counsel involved in the case or any accused. Mr. Hannis, yesterday, indicated that he was going to be accommodating, so far as individual counsel were concerned, even at later stages in the Prosecution case, in the sense that he would accommodate counsel who found difficulty in dealing with a witness because that witness was being introduced at a particular stage. So with that degree of flexibility, I was hoping that we could commence the trial on the 10th of July. Mr. Ackerman has raised certain personal difficulties that that would give him, and there are other personal issues affecting counsel which I have been alerted to and we don't need to elaborate upon here, but having considered any personal difficulties, it seems to me that the -- there are two ways that we can be sure that they won't be -- or that those involved will not be prejudiced. First of all, we have in each case a team representing the accused and, therefore, the individual attendance of lead counsel is not required at every stage. Indeed, I'm in a jurisdiction normally where it's not at all uncommon for appearances to be shared pretty liberally between two counsel representing an accused, and the Court thinks nothing of it. And the second way I think of ensuring that no prejudice is caused is through the alertness of the Judges presiding to ensure that each accused has an entirely fair trial. Now, I know that there may remain concern about these projected dates and I'm now anxious to hear from any counsel who wishes to express that concern. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I'd like to make submissions on where I see the status of this case at this time. I feel that yesterday's 65 ter conference, as you stated at the beginning of this hearing, was very fruitful, and we fully support your proposal to work intensively on an ongoing basis to work towards preparing this case for trial. In relation to a proposed trial date, however, I wish to be candid and direct with you, Your Honour, and to state unequivocally that this case cannot and must not begin this summer. As you indicated to us, this case is not yet assigned to a Trial Chamber, and we ask you to impress upon the powers that be in this institution which do set trial dates and assign Trial Chambers to look at the status of our case. The suggestion of setting this matter for trial this summer, Your Honour, flies in the face of your Trial Chamber decision of the 22nd of March on joinder, and here's why I say that: We have yet no indictment in this case, and a final decision on joinder is forthcoming. We know that on April 5th, the proposed indictment will be filed by the Prosecution, and 15 days after the B/C/S translation we can respond. Then you will rule. That process will probably take us to somewhere in the month of May. Now, what are we to expect in this new proposed indictment or the final indictment when we reach that point? Well, your March 22nd order or decision indicated that there were going to be three important matters which will appear in this new indictment. First, the alleged -- the forces alleged to have perpetrated crimes in Kosovo in 1999, alleged crimes in 1998, and the Joint Command. Your March 22nd decision states that: "The OTP must plead the material facts of these allegations with sufficient specificity to enable the accused to prepare a defence." The addition of these new material facts will cause Mr. Milutinovic unfair prejudice unless he is given an adequate opportunity to prepare an effective defence. The nature and scope of these new material facts significantly broadens this indictment, Your Honour. And let me focus on the 1998 crimes. At a minimum, we must re-examine and analyse all previous disclosure from the Prosecution in relation to 1998. We must re-examine the Milosevic proceedings in light of 1998. We must now review the proceedings in the Limaj case and the Haradinaj case. Both cases pertain to events in Kosovo in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can I just stop you there. Mr. Hannis pointed out yesterday that what this was was an elaboration of paragraph 95 of the third amended indictment. That third amended indictment is dated the 5th of September, 2002. It talks about events beginning in late February 1998. And it deals with allegations of a widespread -- or a campaign of shelling of Kosovo Albanian towns and villages, widespread destruction of property, expulsion of the civilian population. It talks about United Nations's estimates by mid-October 1998 of over 298.000 people, roughly 15 per cent of the population, internally displaced within Kosovo or having left the province. Now, what has changed apart from the possibility that these allegations actually disappear?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, that paragraph is in the section called Additional Facts, I believe, at the tail end of the indictment. And as your decision of the 22nd of March quite rightly points out, that all previous Kosovo indictments and the pre-trial brief from 2004 describes 1998 in what appears to be the least possible detail. Those are the words you wrote. And we agree with that. And now for the first time we can look at -- there's been no -- Milutinovic was given no notice until this joinder indictment was proposed - no meaningful notice - that the crimes in 1998 would be pleaded as material fact. In fact, they were not in the first Milosevic indictment, the Milutinovic indictment, which is seven years old. It was not pleaded in any way materially in the Pavkovic indictment, which is 2003. And the existing indictment was so broad and it covered so many matters that the throw-away paragraph 95, which under the heading of Additional Allegations, or Additional Information, which also includes things going back to 1991 and 1974, if you look at the full array of additional facts, now is -- the Prosecution wants to plead it materially for the reasons it has indicated. Well, that brings it into play for us. So there was no prior notice, Your Honour, in my submission. And certainly we were not going to go to the Registry and say we need additional funds to investigate 1998. They hold our feet to the fire to know exactly what we're doing about 1999, about the indictment. So there is a resources issue involved in this as well. We learned today that there's going to be new disclosure. Fifty new witnesses, seven years down the road. That's one-third of the witnesses the Prosecution intends to call. All these matters require further investigation, and I'm only emphasising the 1998 aspect of the new material facts. But there's more, Your Honour. We are still reviewing crucial material that has been coming to us on a regular basis from the Milosevic proceedings. Since September we have received 10.000 pages. In addition, on CD we received 1.700 MFI documents from the Milosevic proceedings. My submission is that this new proposed -- the proposed indictment containing these new material facts broadens the indictment significantly, and unless Mr. Milutinovic is given adequate time and resources to prepare, his rights to have -- guaranteed to him by Article 21(4)(b) of the Statute will be violated, and we ask you, as the guardian of those rights, to ensure that he gets a fair trial and we are given adequate time to prepare. So we undertake to continue working on this trial to prepare this trial with you as the Pre-Trial Judge, but we are absolutely opposed to an early start-up date. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Defence counsel of the accused Sainovic, I support what Mr. O'Sullivan has just said, and that is the position, I assume, of all the Defence counsel. It is unusual that we today here are discussing the date of the beginning of trial faced with the situation when we have neither the indictment nor disclosure of all the material, when we don't know which Trial Chamber will be hearing the case, and when we are faced in a situation, as I say, which is rather unusual. And if a situation is unusual, it doesn't mean to say that it is impossible. And in supporting everything that Mr. O'Sullivan has just said, I wish to add that I have given it great thought and that I think we should try and find a solution which would lead us to having the trial not begin at this early date but that we don't waste time waiting, to have to meet again at the beginning of next year and then once again take note of the fact that we need more time, and so on and so forth. So, Mr. President, let me repeat publicly what was said less publicly yesterday during the meeting. Our meeting yesterday showed us the way forward, threw light on the way forward which we should progress along. So instead of the trial to start in July, can we introduce a practice to have the meetings held every 15 -- ten to 15 days so that we could go through the 80 witnesses that Mr. Hannis is proposing to hear, to see how much time we'll need for them, who is going -- which one of us is going to conduct the cross-examination, so in effect to have a trial without a trial. And that is a common practice in continental law, in civil law, that this is easily arranged, and so that when we go ahead with the trial, when we have an indictment, when all the deadlines have expired, when we have the pre-trial brief, when we know exactly what we're going to do, that all the time that will seem to have been lost because we take these few months will be made up very rapidly because the trial will be efficient and rapid. And if we discuss all these matters, the witnesses, the experts, and so on and so forth and say that such-and-such a person will be examined by Mr. O'Sullivan during a 20-minute period, we'll stick to that; it will be 20 minutes. You'll have the examination-in-chief plus the 20 minutes. Or we're just going to take the written statement and we won't need to cross-examine a witness at all. So all these matters can be solved by agreement and respecting the principles of a fair and just trial, the resources, and to ensure a fair trial for one and all. So I completely accept what Mr. O'Sullivan has just said and I personally say that it would be very adverse of me to accept something without providing a solution myself. So I think this would be the way forward. It would be a good solution. Thank you, Your Honour. So much from me. I don't want to take up any more of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. O'Sullivan has exhausted all my points, the points on my agenda that I wish to raise. However, there is one piece of information that we were told by Mr. Hannis today that shocked me rather in view of the discussions we held yesterday. The number of new witnesses throws completely new light on my vision of our preparations for the trial to begin, and at this point in time I'm rather confused about all the prognosis for the trial to go ahead in view of what we discussed yesterday and in view of this additional piece of information served to us today when a third or a fourth - I haven't done the calculations exactly - of witnesses we are being given is completely new witnesses, even had we received part of the statements. So as far as I'm concerned, this is a novel situation which demands detailed reorganisation on our part with respect to preparing our defence cases, and that only once we have received the witness statements and once we are disclosed the names of these new witnesses. That's what I wanted to say. Otherwise, I agree fully with all the details set forth by Mr. O'Sullivan and which is the result of our consultations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to Mr. Ackerman and to Your Honour. Just one piece of information that is very important for us for this trial. As you know, Ms. Del Ponte visited Belgrade, and at precisely the day before yesterday, a complete agreement was signed which allows the Prosecution access to all archive material in Serbia and Montenegro. All archives in Serbia and Montenegro. The problem that remains now is for them to know what they're looking for. If they know what they're looking for, then they have the possibility of accessing it as well. And this will complicate our lives additionally when they have access and obtain the documents. This is the first time they have been granted this. They did not have it during your conducting of the Milosevic trial. The agreement was signed the day before yesterday, so this is just a small piece of information that I wanted to put to the Court, and I apologise for taking up more of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- at your invitation, I'd like to supplement a little bit of what I said yesterday. When I left here yesterday, I reflected on -- on some things that you had told me, and one of those specifically was that you were somewhat critical of me for advising you that I really hadn't spent a great deal of time looking at the witness statements and spent too much time looking at Rule 68 material. And in pondering that, what you appeared to be saying to me was that the way to prepare for trial is to read the inculpatory material and forget about the exculpatory. And it's actually just the other way around: How can I possibly cross-examine a Prosecution witness if I haven't found the material necessary to do that cross-examination, which is contained in the Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you know, Mr. Ackerman, that the point I was making is you hardly can realise what exculpatory material you're looking for until you know what the inculpatory material is in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the indictment is pretty clear with regard to all of the crime base stuff as to what the Prosecution's contention is. And I have read some of the witness statements, Your Honour, when it's become important for me to do so. You invited me to put some meat on the bones that I was discussing yesterday, and I'm handicapped by not having all of my material here with me in The Hague. It's mostly back in my office in Texas, but I was able to find a few things, just to give you a sort of thumbnail of the things I am finding in the Rule 68 material. I'm finding witness statements, and I'll mention -- probably better go into closed session because I don't know if these names are protected. And if we can go into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection. I would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into closed session. I'm reminded that that's probably an extreme measure that's not necessary and that private session would be adequate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I get those confused.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on to that subject, is there anyway in which you envisage that the Prosecution can assist with access to witnesses that you identify who may be exculpatory witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. I'm reluctant to even make that request. It -- they certainly might be able to assist me with a current location which I did intend, if we can't locate them, to ask the Prosecution if they know their current location. They may or they may not. I mean, these are people that they have not talked to for years, apparently. But in terms of their assistance in -- I don't know how else they could assist except tell me where they are and how I can contact them. But the Prosecution certainly can't escort me to Kosovo, I don't think. Unless UNMIK says that they can give us safe conduct, safe entrance into Kosovo, then I don't -- I don't have any inclination to go there if it's going to be in danger of my life. And I think that's a serious problem and I think it's a problem that this Tribunal needs to address. Maybe with UNMIK, to take it up with UNMIK as a very formal and official manner, or something, because we can't -- I mean, we can't defend if we can't go there and talk to witnesses. Now, let me go just very briefly to this 54 bis issue. The way the -- the way the Rules read, I'm not -- I'm not permitted to get assistance of the Court until I get refusal from the countries involved. Now, if -- if there's a way to circumvent that and get Court assistance before I get refusal from the countries involved, I'm convinced that would speed matters up. So if that's your position, I need to know it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. You have to obviously make the request in the first place. The real issue is over how long you allow for a response. You don't wait forever for a response. You have to take account of the timetabling of the case and then exercise a judgement about when it's appropriate to invoke the assistance of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the only point I was making. It may be that if a trial is two years away, then you can afford to wait, but if it's impending, then you can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. And what -- what I'll do and what I intend to do in any event in the letter is put a deadline on -- on the letter that I -- that I would like a response by a certain date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what happened in relation to the other litigation we referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, do you wish to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have that happy circumstance, or perhaps unhappy and happy for the other Defence counsel, as fifth Defence counsel, all the topics have been exhausted that I wanted to raise. They are joint topics, and I agreed yesterday with what Mr. Ackerman said at the 65 ter conference when he spoke on the basis of the, conditionally speaking, three new accused and how much time they have to prepare their defence. I today also agree with everything that has been said by Mr. O'Sullivan and indeed by what Mr. Ackerman added. What I wish to add is this: It's a fact that is linked to my client, and I assume that the other accused have a similar problem. We for a year have been collecting documents and evidence to support our case, our defence case, and we're encountering great difficulties in that regard. The Defence of General Lazarevic needed a lot of time to identify a certain amount of documents. This took a long time, and then to address in official terms the archives through the ministerial council and the Centre for Cooperation with The Hague Tribunal for gaining access to those documents. In January, as early as January, the Defence put in a request for identified documents but up till the present day we have not received a single one of those. Now, in view of the fact that we're discussing the beginning of trial here and that we have pinpointed the month of July as a possibility, it is quite evident that in addition to what my colleagues Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Ackerman have already said yesterday and today, that this will be an additional problem that we have to face, that is to say that the Defence has to prepare for the start of trial and the time it will need, and that is why I say I agree fully with what my colleagues Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Ackerman have already stated, as well as Mr. Fila, of course, my colleague Mr. Fila who asked that the start of trial be postponed. And I fully endorse and support the fact that we could have more frequent 65 ter meetings, perhaps, which would be more expeditious in the long-run. It would lead to a more expeditious and rational trial rather than having the start of trial be on the 10th of July. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. The comment I made to Mr. Ackerman about invoking the assistance of the Court under Rule 54 bis would apply in particular to the situation that you've just outlined where an application or a request for assistance made in January has still elicited no response. In my view, that's more than ample time for a response. So it's a matter for you, but I suggest that action is required in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe there has been a misunderstanding. We don't have a negative answer. It's a matter of technical possibilities, complicated procedures, approvals to be granted, the whole paperwork that these documents have to go through in order for us to receive them. The problem is that not that we won't get the approval but that these documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I admire your patience. It's a gift I'm not endowed with, I'm afraid. Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Lukic Defence whole-heartedly concurs with the statements made by our colleagues here today and we wish just to underscore and highlight certain issues of particular importance to our defence that illustrate the need -- the concerns that everyone has voiced regarding a trial date in early July. First, I would highlight that although the Trial Chamber in August and December envisioned Defence counsel to have complete access to the materials from the Milosevic case, outside factors have prevented the various Defences from obtaining those documents on a time schedule that had then been anticipated. By way of example, my Defence team just yesterday, five minutes before the 65 ter conference, and then only with the assistance of the associate legal officer, whom I have to thank very heartily, were provided with the Milosevic exhibits on a portable hard drive, which we now have access to and we can now review. I'm told that the quantity of those documents comprises approximately 9.5 gigabites on the hard drive, which is I don't know how many thousands of pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that this is all the exhibits in the Milosevic case? This is your first access to the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why was there a delay in giving you these?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The delay was in terms of, it's my understanding that the exhibits, according to the Registry, were on the JDB database which, unfortunately, our Defence team still does not have access to. This morning, the latest communication from the Registry that I received indicated that although our key, our decoder key for the JDB, had been issued in December, that due to a misunderstanding it had not been authorised to access. So as of this morning I still cannot remotely access JDB unless I'm present on the premises of the Tribunal at one of the local area network connected computers to do so. Which, of course, causes quite a dilemma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you knew this in December, why did you not do something about it earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have been liaising with the Registry since then to try and resolve this matter, and as I indicated, they indicated it would now be resolved. But more importantly, with regards to material that we have been working with on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Ivetic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You did hear the message -- you perhaps haven't. The interpreter is asking you to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will endeavour to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the material, I believe some of the material that Mr. Bakrac was referencing is material that we are also seeking from the Serbian government. I'm particular with respect to my client. We have been asking for material from the various MUP archives that we know exist since my client was an employee of the MUP for many years and which we believe provides very exculpatory material for our client, and we're told that this material may comprise as much as 30 to 40.000 pages. We have been working with the Serbian authorities to try and gain access to this material, but it has been slow in coming due to the multitude of the material and technical aspects of providing it to us. I am told, as far as that material is concerned, that we have now been given approximately four out of 12 categories of material, all of which, based upon our knowledge of what should be there, are very relevant to our defence and exculpatory for General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give me an example?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honour. There are records pertaining to efforts undertaken by the MUP following the Kosovo conflict to investigate allegations of crimes that occurred within the premises of Kosovo and Metohija, crimes that were committed perhaps by civilians, perhaps by MUP personnel, perhaps by army personnel, et cetera. This information relates to investigations that were undertaken, some of which my client was personally involved in, and the charges that were presented or evidence that was presented to the state Prosecutor's office to actually charge and prosecute these individuals for war crimes within the Serbian government and within the Serbian judicial system. In fact, there have been reports in -- that I've seen in the news pertaining to particular cases that were brought in Serbia that I know were initiated by my client and were the fruits of this labour that was undertaken by the MUP and that this documentation would be very crucial to our defence in terms of establishing the -- establishing that there is no criminal responsibility for my client for the charges alleged within the indictment. So that is one of the areas that we have been having issues with. The second outside factor that needs to be taken into account is the Registry and the manner in which the Registry provides for the defence of these cases. Now, the Registry in I believe it was in January of this year indicated that on their estimation and based upon their judgement the resources for the Lukic Defence were to be spread out over a nine-month period in this year because that was their indication of the minimum time period required to prepare for the defence. Similarly, in August of last year, as part of our work plan, we requested that a co-counsel be provided for this case. The Registry has steadfastly indicated that, pursuant to their guidelines, co-counsel will not be provided until five months prior to the start of trial, and thus as of today's date, our team officially does not have a co-counsel, which is why I request special permission to be present in lieu of Mr. Scudder today. Now, the difficulty that that provides is primarily in respect to travel insofar as co-counsel and counsel are granted leeway to travel and meet with investigators and conduct defence-related activities on behalf of the Defence team. Other members of the Defence team, such as myself, are not granted such precedence or leeway by the Registry. Your Honour will recall that in the proceedings, the 65 ter and the status that occurred in December of 2005, I was not present. That is because my travel request was denied by the Registry. We have issues like this arising time and time again where, in order to travel to Belgrade, as I did in December after the date of the Status Conference, I had to expend personal funds to do so. And that hampers the ability of the Lukic Defence to competently prepare for and attain a level of readiness for a trial in early July of this year. And I would only ask that the Trial Chamber be aware of many of these outside factors that have hampered, I believe, not just our Defence but the Defence of the other two individuals who are "recent" additions to these proceedings. So those are just some of the issues that I wish to highlight with respect to the difficulties that the Defence has had in preparation and that we foresee will continue to hamper our abilities and would make it difficult for us to be professionally and ethically able to declare our readiness for trial in early July of 2006. And I just highlight the concerns that Mr. Ackerman made yesterday with respect to, from our jurisdiction in the United States, whether we can ethically and professionally do so, given the fact that we know that there's material we have not received and will not have an opportunity to review in time for the July trial date. And I thank the Court for its time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have just a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic reminded me of something I was going to apprise you of and neglected to do so. At this stage, my assignment in this case remains temporary. So I'm not permanently assigned to this case yet. And that's because the Registry has spent these many months investigating the financial resources of my client and still have not come to a decision as to whether he must contribute to his own defence in some way. That's a particular problem for counsel from America. I don't know if you're aware of it, but there is a regulation by the United States Treasury Department that would prohibit me from accepting any funds from anyone charged with a war crime in this Tribunal, and we encountered that problem in a previous case here and got it solved, but it was in a completely different context. In this context, there's no doubt but what I would be absolutely be prohibited from accepting any funds whatsoever from -- from Mr. Pavkovic. And if the Registry were to determine that he was responsible for, say, half of my compensation, then I would simply have to withdraw from the case. I don't think I'd have much choice, and that could create huge problems. The only alternative is that you can make application to the Treasury Department for a waiver, but sometimes those take many, many months to get dealt with. So that's where we are in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Now, Mr. Hannis, do you wish to address this issue at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I will take account of the submissions that have been made when I draft the work plan, which will include the projected dates for various events, including the trial commencement, and I'll deal with that in an order which will be issued next week. I can indicate now that it's unlikely to be significantly different from the indication I gave except that it's likely to be far more detailed, and that's because some of the submissions which have been made just now behind which there is greatest force depend to some extent on developments which have yet to occur, but the intensity of management of the case will be such that there will be plenty of opportunity to reflect upon and submit about the developments in the case as they occur. Now, that completes my agenda for this Status Conference. Are there any matters that -- any additional matters that any Defence counsel wish to raise? Thank you. Mr. Hannis, is there anything else you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I simply conclude by expressing my gratitude to everybody for their continued cooperation in the efforts we're making to have this case heard, and I look forward to our next meeting, which will be along the lines of the time scale discussed earlier, I anticipate sometime in the week beginning the 24th of April.
